title: Designing a Deterministic Safety Cage for an ML Lunar Lander
description: A runtime architecture that validates ML landing commands against physical constraints in a lunar-landing simulator, with OOD detection, physics cross-checks and deterministic fallback.
author: Embedded AI & ML Verification Engineer (portfolio author)
seoTitle: A Deterministic Safety Cage for an ML Lunar Lander — Engineering Note
seoDescription: Runtime validation of ML guidance outputs: ODD, physics estimators, deterministic constraints, FMEA and fault injection in simulation.

content.title: 1. Why an ML Output Should Not Be Trusted Unconditionally

content.text: An ML guidance model is learned, not proved. Even a well-tested model can output an absurd command outside its training regime. A deterministic safety cage sits between the ML output and the actuator path and applies hard, checkable constraints before any command is released.

The reference system is a synthetic lunar-landing simulator: camera and inertial state feed an ML guidance estimator; the cage validates commands against physical and operational constraints; a deterministic fallback controller takes over when needed. This is an engineering demonstration environment, not a flight system.

The ODD fixes altitude, velocity, fuel-margin and terrain bounds, plus supported modes. Explicit prohibited regions exist: any command that would violate a hard constraint, and any use of the ML output without the cage.
Raw inputs are range-checked before they reach the estimators. Incoherent or out-of-range sensor readings are handled by validation and fallback, never silently fused.

Terrain and state features outside the trained regime raise an OOD flag. The cage responds by rejecting the ML command and engaging fallback. In the reference campaign the OOD detection rate reached 0.94.
The ML component proposes guidance commands (vertical and horizontal velocity, throttle). It is treated as a candidate generator, not as the authority.

An independent, deterministic physics estimator projects the trajectory from state and fuel. It shares preprocessing with the ML model in the reference design — an identified common-mode weakness, not a hidden strength.
ML and physics estimates are compared. Divergence beyond a configured limit rejects the ML command. This is a detection mechanism, and its common-mode dependence is documented as a residual risk.
Altitude ceiling, vertical velocity, horizontal velocity, fuel margin and projected touchdown velocity are enforced by explicit, reviewable comparisons — no learned thresholds in the cage.
Every rejected command is logged with the violated constraint. In the Monte Carlo campaign (500 synthetic profiles), 12 unsafe commands were caught and zero violations were released.
Fallback is a deterministic pre-planned guidance profile, activated within 100 ms. It does not depend on the ML component.
The cage and fallback have explicit time budgets. On delay injection the fallback activated at 74 ms median in simulation.
Sensor dropout triggers the pre-planned fallback. Incoherent sensors revealed plan-selection oscillation — a real finding that motivates hysteresis and plan-locking as mitigations.
Absurd ML outputs (out of range) are rejected; all 40 injected absurd commands in the campaign were rejected.
Model bit flips are simulated via fault injection; the cage and physics estimator provide a second line of defence when flips change outputs plausibly.

The strongest residual risk is shared preprocessing between ML and physics estimator: if both fail from the same cause, the cage may validate a wrong command. The independence review is INCONCLUSIVE until preprocessing is decoupled.

Failure modes cover unsafe output accepted, valid command rejected, fallback delayed, OOD missed and common-mode failure, each linked to requirements, tests and evidence. The FMEA is a synthetic engineering example requiring project-specific review.
Automated scenarios covered sensor dropout, sensor noise, incoherent sensors, terrain OOD, delayed inference, invalid outputs and model bit flips, each mapped to a requirement and a verdict.

Common-mode failure requires mitigation before any real use; simulator simplification requires independent V&V and hardware-in-the-loop; false rejection is accepted with limitations at the demonstration threshold.

items: Demonstration / simulation: CONDITIONAL_GO.
Hardware-in-the-loop: REVIEW_REQUIRED (not yet performed).
Real operational flight: NO_GO without independent V&V and complete HIL qualification.

content.text: Monitor rejected commands, fallback activations, ML-vs-physics divergence, OOD events and constraint violations. The operational invariant: released constraint violations must remain zero.
Before any claim beyond simulation, run the cage on target hardware with real sensor timing, evaluate fallback timing end-to-end, and repeat the Monte Carlo sweep on the target.

Common-mode preprocessing dependency open.
Fallback oscillation on incoherent sensors (mitigation in progress).

All results obtained in a synthetic or simulated engineering environment.
ODD with explicit prohibited regions
Deterministic constraints reviewable by humans
Independent physics estimate with documented dependencies

Monte Carlo sweep with zero released violations
Common-mode analysis performed
Deployment decision separated per environment

content.text: A deterministic safety cage converts an ML guidance model into a component whose outputs are constrained by physics and reviewed before release. Its value is proven in simulation; its honesty is the explicit list of what simulation did not prove.
